A_target.statement:
Let $T$ be an [[Definition:Infinite Set|infinite]] [[Definition:Rooted Tree|rooted tree]] in which every [[Definition:Vertex of Graph|vertex]] has finitely many children.
Then $T$ has an infinite [[Definition:Path (Graph Theory)|path]] starting at the root.

B_source.statement:
Let $S$ be an [[Definition:Infinite Set|infinite set]] partitioned into finitely many classes $S_1, \ldots, S_k$.
Then some $S_i$ is infinite.

substitutions.the objects being classified: the nodes lying below a given node
substitutions.the finitely many boxes: the finitely many children of that node
substitutions.the infinite box: the child with infinitely many descendants

derived.one application selecting an infinite cl: one step of the path, selecting a child with infinitely many descendants
derived.the conclusion of a single application: an infinite path, obtained by iterating the selection

validity_conditions: Finite branching is what makes the pigeonhole step available, since it supplies finitely many classes at each node.
The invariant maintained is that the current node has infinitely many descendants, which is exactly what lets the step repeat forever.

The selection at each stage requires a choice among the children; for arbitrary trees this uses a weak choice principle, though for trees with an ordering on children the choice can be made canonically.
proof_plan:
Let $v_0$ be the root.
As $T$ is infinite, $v_0$ has infinitely many descendants.

Classify the descendants of $v_0$ according to which of its finitely many children they pass through.
By the [[Infinite Pigeonhole Principle]], some child $v_1$ has infinitely many descendants.

Move to $v_1$.
The invariant, that the current vertex has infinitely many descendants, is preserved.
